newsitem.title: JAPAN: Russia tries to break deadlock over disputed isles.
newsitem.headline: Russia tries to break deadlock over disputed isles.

text.p: Russia on Friday tried to break a decades-long deadlock with Japan over islands both nations claim by formally proposing they jointly develop their rich mineral and fishery resources.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov made the proposal in talks with Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, ministry officials said.
"In the talks, the Russian side formally proposed a 'Joint Economic Activities Programme' over the islands," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement. There were no details.

Primakov also proposed the joint development of the islands during an earlier meeting with ex-premier Yasuhiro Nakasone and Taku Yamazaki, policy chief of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), LDP officials said.

The row over the islands, called the Southern Kuriles by Russia and the Northern Territories by Japan, has stopped the two countries from signing a formal World War Two peace treaty and frozen bilateral ties for most of the last 50 years.

With Japan also involved in disputes with China, Taiwan and South Korea in separate island disputes, the Russian proposal was likely to get a cautious response from Tokyo in case it affected those disputes.
"I would like to propose the joint development of the four islands, without damaging the basic positions of both Russia and Japan," LDP officials quoted Primakov as telling Nakasone.
Ikeda and Primakov reaffirmed their commitment to the 1993 Tokyo Declaration, which said the two countries would resolve the dispute based on "law and justice", ministry officials said.
Primakov was also scheduled to meet with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and address a news conference where he was expected to reveal details of his proposal.
The islands of Etorofu, Kunashiri and Shikotan, and the Habomai group, were seized by the advancing Soviet army in the closing days of World War Two.
Russia says the islands were part of territory promised to them at the Yalta Conference of World War Two allies.
But Japan has insisted the four islands have belonged to it as far back as 1856 when the Tokugawa Shogunate signed its first treaty with Czarist Russia.
The Soviet government under Josef Stalin heavily favoured the volcanic islands, rich in mineral and fishery resources, offering lucrative wages to potential Russian immigrants.

In 1956, when the two countries normalised ties, the Kremlin offered to revert two islands to Japan upon conclusion of a World War Two peace treaty and then discuss the future of the other two after that.
But when Japan signed the 1960 U.S.-Japan Security Treaty, Moscow annulled the 1956 pledge, and until the late 1980s insisted that a territorial issue did not exist at all.
A new phase came with Russian President Boris Yeltsin's visit to Tokyo in 1993 when he admitted there was a dispute and promised to settle it based on "law and justice".
With the breakup of the Soviet Union and ensuing economic woes, the 20,000-population islands, often hit by earthquakes, have become a backwater in Russian economic development plans.
But ever fearful of a nationalist backlash if it gave too much ground on the issue, Russia until now has been as stubborn as Japan in refusing to budge on its claims.

With the existing stalemate, the waters around the islands have become the scene of frequent minor clashes between Japanese fishermen and Russian coastguard boats, occasionally leading to seizure of trawlers.
